title: Hurricane Polo surf: Orange County flood advisory runs to Wednesday
dek: Hurricane Polo's swell brought 4 to 7 foot surf to south-facing SoCal beaches. An Orange County coastal flood advisory lasts until 5 p.m. Wednesday.
keyPoints: Orange County beaches: coastal flood advisory until 5 p.m. Wednesday, per the National Weather Service.
Ventura and Los Angeles County coastal flood and high surf advisories were set to end at 5 p.m. Tuesday.
Surf of 4 to 7 feet hit south-facing beaches, with late-morning high tides near 7 feet.
Long Beach sandbags: Claremont Parking Lot, 5400 E. Ocean Blvd; LA County residents can check LAFD stations.

sources.title: Hurricane Polo Swells Bring High Surf, Coastal Flooding Concerns - MyNewsLA.com
Hurricane Polo expected to bring strong swells to Southern California, prompting coastal flood advisory - CBS Los Angeles
Swells from Hurricane Polo bring high surf, coastal flooding threat to Long Beach | FOX 11 Los Angeles

body: Hurricane Polo stayed well south of California, and its swell still reached Southern California this week. The National Weather Service forecast surf of 4 to 7 feet at south-facing beaches on Monday and Tuesday, with late-morning high tides near 7 feet, close to a foot above normal. Avalon, Long Beach and Malibu were named as the areas of greatest concern.

The coastal flood and high surf advisories for Ventura and Los Angeles County beaches were set to expire at 5 p.m. Tuesday. In Orange County, the high surf advisory also ended Tuesday evening, and the coastal flood advisory stays in effect until 5 p.m. Wednesday. Fox 11 reported that southerly swells from Polo and Hurricane Odalys could affect coastal waters through about midweek.

Forecasters warned of shallow seawater flooding on walkways, parking lots and roads near the beach, significant erosion, and widespread, very strong rip currents. The weather service also noted that the surf would likely be smaller than during Hurricane Marie, though erosion left by that storm could make flooding worse. Its advice is to stay out of the water, stay off rock jetties, and protect property in flood-prone spots.

If you live near the water, sandbags are available. Long Beach has pre-filled and empty bags at the Claremont Parking Lot, 5400 E. Ocean Blvd, and Los Angeles County residents can check Los Angeles Fire Department stations. The LAFD website, lafd.org, explains how to place them.
If you are heading to an Orange County beach before Wednesday afternoon, check the late-morning high tide, park away from low lots near the sand, and watch the surf from dry ground.
